quote: PIPs would be responsible for carrying out ID checks, as is done for bank accounts. Users would therefore be identifiable to the wallet providers, but they would be anonymous to the Bank and the Government.
actor: CB (core-ledger operator); identity held by PIPs
modality: conditional: if a digital pound is introduced; legislation to guarantee privacy
justification: The competent bodies (BoE/HMT) state in the 2024 Consultation Response that users would be anonymous to the Bank. This is an architectural statement, not only a 'will not use' pledge. PIPs anonymise personal data before transactions are settled by the Bank (doc 4 p. 10), and the Bank receives payment messages in anonymised form (doc 3 p. 57). The 2026 progress update says safeguards are structural rather than dependent on restraint (doc 17 p. 7). The cell is partial, not documented, because the qualifier 'CB holds no routine key to identity' is not established. Technical prevention of Bank access is still only being explored (doc 4 p. 30; doc 17 p. 6), and the Bank-run alias repository may hold personal data (doc 10 p. 13).
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 30: A.2. The Bank commits to exploring technological options that would prevent the Bank from accessing any personal data through the Bank’s core infrastructure.

quote: Private-sector digital pound wallet providers, Payment Interface Providers (PIPs), would anonymise personal data before transactions are processed and settled by the Bank.
actor: PSP (PIPs); payer and payee each identifiable to own PIP
modality: conditional: if a digital pound is introduced
justification: The value is inferred under §6.5 within one design version (2024 Consultation Response), for the same participant (the user's PIP) in online mode. The three premises are: (i) the PIP holds the identity mapping (doc 4 p. 28, p. 45); (ii) the PIP holds the user's transaction data (doc 4 p. 30); (iii) the PIP handles personal data together with the transaction before anonymising it for settlement (doc 4 p. 10). The explicit Technology Working Paper statement 'not privacy from their PIPs' corroborates this as an option (doc 2 p. 56). The PoC shows payer and payee PIPs both see transaction data, as tested (doc 6 p. 22).
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 46: privacy-preserving alias service which would ... also limit the sharing of personal data between users and PIPs.

quote: In addition to law enforcement to fight crime (operating via law enforcement agencies engaging with PIPs under rules already approved by Parliament and not directly with the Bank), these are likely to be limited to:
modality: conditional: under existing rules approved by Parliament; lawful, proportionate and fair case, challengeable by wallet provider (doc 4 p. 43); further scenarios via a data framework to be presented to Parliament (doc 4 p. 30)
justification: The most specific adopted statement names PIPs as the holder that law enforcement engages with and excludes direct access via the Bank. The value is therefore via_PSP, not via_both. Earlier 'prescribed in law' sentences that do not name a holder (doc 2 p. 21; doc 3 p. 16) would alone give n/d, but they are refined here. The 'no Bank or Government access' statements (doc 9 p. 3) concern the Bank route and do not conflict with a PSP route.
counter_evidence: doc 9 p. 3: guaranteeing that neither the Bank nor the Government could access users’ personal information

quote: To do this, the digital pound design would enable deferred offline payments − where the payment goes through sometime after the transaction is initiated, for example once one party is back online or via submitting a batch of files for overnight payment processing.
transaction_scope: offline (deferred; device offline not expected at launch)
modality: exploratory design note; not final policy
justification: There is no adopted offline commitment and no adopted decision against offline. The offline report says no final decision has been made (doc 12 p. 3), and the latest design note is exploratory (doc 16 p. 3). The envisaged deferred mode settles on the ledger later, but whether transfer details are linked to a person at synchronisation is not described. Under the 'offline without privacy description → unknown' rule this stays n/d rather than no. The PET-based private synchronisation is only a tested capability (doc 12 p. 11).
counter_evidence: doc 12 p. 11: it was technically feasible to store an offline transaction record while protecting personal data when users reconnected to the network.

quote: Just like opening a bank or other payment account, some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound
modality: conditional: if a digital pound is introduced
justification: The adopted requirement applies to opening any digital pound wallet, and the same document states the digital pound would not be anonymous (doc 4 p. 28). The §6.6a inference cannot be used, because lower-identification tiers are mentioned (doc 3 p. 77; doc 4 p. 46). Those tiers are described as 'limited identity verification', which is KYC-lite and not a no-identity route (doc 3 p. 77). The cell is partial because tiered access 'based on the amount of identification a user is willing or able to provide' is still being explored without stated limits (doc 4 p. 46).
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 46: committed to exploring how PIPs could offer tiered access to users, with functionality based on the amount of identification a user is willing or able to provide.

quote: Just like opening a bank or other payment account, some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound
modality: conditional: if a digital pound is introduced
justification: The adopted Consultation Response requires identity verification at wallet opening. It adds that PIPs carry out ID checks as for bank accounts (doc 4 p. 45). This is consistent with the Consultation Paper (doc 3 p. 76) and later design notes (doc 13 p. 5; doc 14 p. 7). No document states a standard wallet without verification.

quote: In addition to law enforcement to fight crime (operating via law enforcement agencies engaging with PIPs under rules already approved by Parliament and not directly with the Bank), these are likely to be limited to:
actor: law enforcement agencies via PIPs (not via the Bank)
modality: conditional: rules approved by Parliament; lawful, proportionate and fair case, challengeable by wallet provider (doc 4 p. 43); possible further scenarios such as unresolved disputes via FOS (doc 4 p. 31, option)
justification: The adopted text documents attribution of transactions to persons under extraordinary conditions. This is done by law enforcement through PIPs, not through the Bank. The condition is a lawful, proportionate and fair case (doc 4 p. 43). An earlier option-level statement 'except for law enforcement ... prescribed in law' corroborates this (doc 3 p. 16).

quote: Neither the Bank nor the Government will program the public’s money or control their spending.
modality: unconditional; to be prohibited by primary legislation and made technically impossible (doc 17 p. 7)
justification: State- and issuer-imposed programmability is ruled out consistently, from the Consultation Paper (doc 3 p. 83) through the Consultation Response (doc 4 p. 33) to the 2026 update. Programmability that remains is user-requested and consent-based (doc 4 p. 32; doc 18 p. 6), which the contract distinguishes from state restrictions. Holding limits (doc 4 p. 53) are balance caps, not use restrictions.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p. 53: minded to proceed at this stage with a proposed holding limit in the range of £10,000 to £20,000

quote: Interoperability between forms of money is also key to achieving the two primary motivations in considering a digital pound, as set out in the consultation paper: (a) preserving access to retail public money as a universal, financially risk-free asset in an increasingly digital economy, and (b) supporting innovation, choice and efficiency across the UK payments system.
justification: Efficiency and choice in payments is part of primary motivation (b), declared since the Consultation Paper (doc 3 p. 28) and restated in 2026. The 2026 update also frames the decision against other initiatives to modernise payments (doc 17 p. 1).

quote: Determine whether a digital pound, as proposed in the blueprint, will meet the Bank and HM Treasury’s objectives of supporting the singleness of money while fostering competition, innovation, choice in payments and supporting financial inclusion.
justification: Inclusion is declared as an objective, though a secondary one. Supporting sources are the 'other motivations' in the Consultation Paper (doc 3 p. 29), the Consultation Response (doc 4 p. 57) and the 2025 objectives list. The institution notes its limited potential in the UK (doc 3 p. 91). The 2026 core objectives omit inclusion and treat it as a do-no-harm constraint (doc 17 p. 3), which weakens the flag, but they do not withdraw it.
counter_evidence: doc 17 p. 3: It should also not exacerbate financial exclusion.

quote: To sustain access to UK central bank money – ensuring its role as an anchor for confidence and safety in our monetary system, and to underpin monetary and financial stability and sovereignty
justification: Monetary sovereignty and the anchor role of public money are part of primary motivation (a). This is restated as 'singleness of money' (doc 9 p. 11; doc 11 p. 5) and 'sovereignty' (doc 4 p. 18). Policy transmission is explicitly not a motivation (doc 3 p. 45), but the flag is satisfied by the sovereignty component.
counter_evidence: doc 3 p. 45: using the digital pound as an additional tool for the transmission of monetary policy is not a policy motivation for it.

quote: There are other motivations for developing the digital pound. These include supporting financial inclusion and improving domestic payments resilience and cross-border payments.
justification: Payments resilience is declared as a secondary motivation (doc 3 p. 29, p. 40). It is restated as resilience through diversity of payment options (doc 9 p. 6). Continued public access to public money as cash declines also appears (doc 9 p. 10; doc 11 p. 5). The digital pound is a complement to cash, not a replacement (doc 4 p. 33), and a later design note calls resilience 'not a core motivation' (doc 16 p. 7). The flag is therefore secondary and medium confidence.
counter_evidence: doc 16 p. 7: Although is it not a core motivation, enhancing resilience has been noted as a potential benefit of the digital pound.

quote: Given laws to fight financial crime, it would not be anonymous.
justification: AML/CFT appears only as a design requirement or constraint (doc 1 p. 23; doc 14 p. 18; doc 17 p. 7). Under the F11 trap, a requirement is not a declared objective. No finding declares enforcement as an objective. The zero flag means 'not documented as objective in the checked sources'.

quote: One of the digital pound’s principal aims is to support payments innovation by the private sector.
justification: Innovation and competition form part of primary motivation (b) throughout. Sources include doc 4 p. 58, doc 11 p. 5 and doc 17 p. 4, and the 2026 core objectives of 'fostering competition, innovation and choice' (doc 17 p. 3).

quote: Interoperability between forms of money is also key to achieving the two primary motivations in considering a digital pound, as set out in the consultation paper: (a) preserving access to retail public money as a universal, financially risk-free asset in an increasingly digital economy, and (b) supporting innovation, choice and efficiency across the UK payments system.
justification: Two motivations are explicitly labelled 'primary' and are not ranked against each other (doc 3 p. 28; doc 4 p. 58; doc 15 p. 7; doc 17 p. 4). Other motivations are labelled secondary. The value is several_joint, not unranked, because a ranking above the secondary objectives is documented.
counter_evidence: doc 8 p. 7: ensuring that the digital pound, if introduced, would promote further choice, competition, efficiency and innovation in the evolving payments landscape.

value: (a) preserving access to retail public money as anchor / singleness of money (monetary and financial stability and sovereignty); (b) supporting innovation, choice and efficiency across the UK payments system
quote: Interoperability between forms of money is also key to achieving the two primary motivations in considering a digital pound, as set out in the consultation paper: (a) preserving access to retail public money as a universal, financially risk-free asset in an increasingly digital economy, and (b) supporting innovation, choice and efficiency across the UK payments system.
justification: The latest official restatement of the two primary motivations is consistent with the Consultation Paper (doc 3 p. 28) and the Consultation Response (doc 4 p. 58). The 2026 core objectives phrase them as singleness of money plus competition, innovation and choice (doc 17 p. 3).

quote: We are continuing our evaluations of various ledger technologies and architectures, including relational databases, NoSQL and distributed ledger technologies, to determine their ability to meet technical requirements
justification: No ledger technology has been chosen. The 2023 preference for centrally governed distributed databases was explicitly kept open (doc 2 p. 52; doc 5 p. 18). In 2026 technological choices are deferred to the forthcoming blueprint (doc 17 p. 3). The centralised Lab demonstration ledger and the Hyperledger Cacti bridge are tested only (doc 18 p. 9), which by rule is not an adoption. Permissioned operation is required (doc 1 p. 46) and proof of work is excluded (doc 2 p. 45).
counter_evidence: doc 18 p. 9: the purchase is initiated on a blockchain ledger, then confirmed on the demonstration ledger, which is centralised.
